No. Your bag is on the chair. The apron is next to the door.

Can you help me put these books away at four?
I have a music lesson then, but I can come at five.
That works. Please use the side door. The front door closes at half past four.
What will the second speaker do?

I found a notebook for Ben, but he already has three.
How about a small plant? He likes growing things.
Good idea. We can buy one after lunch.

The poster looks good, but the phone number has one wrong digit.
I will correct it tonight. Can you print it tomorrow morning?
The printer will be checked tomorrow. I can print it this afternoon if you fix it now.
All right. Give me ten minutes.
What will happen next?

Our centre used to give visitors a map with only street names. Some visitors still got lost because they did not know where the streets began. We have now added drawings of the bakery and the clock tower. The route itself has not changed. We hope the familiar buildings will make the map easier to use.
Why were drawings added to the map?

jobs.text:
Our repair workshop has twelve bookings, but we have only eight sets of tools.
We could buy four more sets.
The budget is fixed. What if we divide the visitors into two groups and let one group watch the safety demonstration first?
That would work. We can exchange the groups after half an hour.
What solution do the speakers agree on?

Thank you for using our seed exchange. Last month, many packets came back without the plant names. This made sorting difficult. From next week, please put the empty packet inside the return box even if you have used all the seeds. There is no need to write a separate note; the name printed on the packet is enough.
What are users asked to do?

jobs.text:
Our online survey says the evening study room is popular. Should we add more evening sessions?
Perhaps, but people who cannot get home late may never have answered. The survey link was displayed inside the study room.
Then we should ask students outside the room as well before deciding.
Yes. Otherwise we might improve the service only for those who already use it.
What do the speakers decide to do first?

Our walking group has produced a route map with estimated journey times. Please remember that these times were measured by experienced members carrying no luggage. Before we publish the map widely, we would like volunteers who walk at different speeds to test it. We may give a range of times instead of one figure. The route will stay the same; the aim is to make the advice more useful to different walkers.
Why does the group want more volunteers to test the map?

jobs.text:
The new booking app has a very high satisfaction score. Can we replace the remaining telephone service?
I would hesitate. Those scores come from people who completed a booking. We have no information from those who gave up.
So a high score does not necessarily mean the service works for everyone.
Exactly. We should examine failed attempts and talk to the telephone users before making a decision.
What is the second speaker’s main concern?

Our centre used less electricity this summer than last summer. This may sound like evidence that the new lights saved a great deal of energy. However, the centre was also closed for two weeks, and the weather was cooler. We will compare electricity use during similar opening hours before estimating the contribution of the lights. This does not mean the lights were ineffective; it means the total reduction cannot all be attributed to them yet.
Why is the speaker delaying a conclusion about the lights?

jobs.text:
In the pilot district, missed appointments declined after the reminder messages were introduced. Can we recommend the system across the region?
The result is encouraging, but the pilot also changed how easily appointments could be rescheduled. We do not know which change mattered more.
Would it be better to expand in stages and compare districts with different combinations?
Yes, provided we do not treat the districts as identical. We should record differences in transport access and in the people served.
Which approach does the second speaker support?

The new service target requires our advice team to respond within one working day. This has reduced the number of requests left unanswered for weeks. However, the target counts an initial acknowledgement as a response. A quick message saying that a request has been received may be useful, but it does not show whether the underlying problem has been addressed. Our next report will therefore distinguish acknowledgement from substantive guidance and track whether clients need to make repeated requests. We are supplementing the speed measure, not suggesting that prompt replies are unimportant.
What is the speaker’s main point?
